html:
The first permanent stone theatre in Rome, built by Pompey on the Campus Martius and opened in 55 BCE.

For centuries the Senate had banned permanent theatres as bad for morals, so plays were staged on wooden stands that were taken down afterwards. Pompey got round this by putting a temple of Venus Victrix at the top of the seating, so the curved rows could be called the temple's steps.

Behind the stage stretched a long garden with colonnades, fountains and statues, one of the first public parks in Rome. At its far end was a meeting hall, the Curia of Pompey, where the Senate sometimes met. There, on the Ides of March 44 BCE, Julius Caesar was stabbed to death, falling at the foot of Pompey's statue (see assassination of Julius Caesar).

Little of it now stands above ground. Its curve survives in the shape of the streets and houses near Campo de' Fiori, and remains of the Curia lie in the Largo di Torre Argentina. Later Rome built far bigger venues, like the Colosseum.
sum: The first permanent stone theatre in Rome, built by Pompey on the Campus Martius and opened in 55 BCE.
